The FOMC statement acknowledges that COVID-19 will depress near-term activity and elevate downside risks, but it pairs that assessment with an unusually forceful easing package that the literature suggests can materially cushion the shock. Consistent with the credit view and financial accelerator (Bernanke-Gertler; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein; Gertler and Gilchrist), large Treasury/MBS purchases, expanded repos, discount window relief, and swap lines should lower the external finance premium and stabilize bank-dependent and small-firm credit. VAR evidence on monetary transmission (Sims) and the Taylor principle support front-loaded cuts to the ELB when demand collapses and inflation is below target; with market-based inflation compensation falling and surveys roughly anchored, inflation-bias/time-inconsistency concerns (Rogoff; Svensson) are limited. At the ELB, QE and liquidity backstops operate through market-functioning, term-premium, and expectations channels and help repair global dollar funding (Oliner and Rudebusch), aligning with the Fed’s dual-mandate objectives. Net, the outlook remains negative in the near term, but the announced toolkit should mitigate amplification via credit channels and support a gradual return toward maximum employment and price stability.
